claims.text: Kubernetes ships no Pod networking of its own: a CNI plugin, installed on the nodes, is required to implement the Kubernetes network model; Kubernetes (API server, kubelet) records and reports the Pod address but does not assign it or move packets.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Extend Kubernetes > Network Plugins (overview: 'A CNI plugin is required to implement the Kubernetes network model'); Cluster Networking

claims.text: The container runtime (asked by the kubelet to start containers) loads and calls the CNI plugin when a Pod is created; the plugin gives the Pod its IP and connects it to the node; once sandbox and network are set up the Pod is ready to start containers (PodReadyToStartContainers).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Plugins > Installation ('the Container Runtime must be configured to load the CNI plugins'); Pod conditions (PodReadyToStartContainers)

claims.text: The kubelet reports the Pod's IP address to the API server, where it appears in status.podIP.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Pod API reference (PodStatus.podIP); Concepts > Workloads > Pods

claims.text: Without a CNI plugin, Pods that use the Pod network cannot be connected and the kubelet reports the node NotReady. Some tools (kind) install a plugin while building the cluster; with others the person building the cluster installs it separately.
claims.source_hint: Proposed prompt 08 capture (repo_changes_needed): kind, disableDefaultCNI, kubectl get nodes; kubernetes.io: kubeadm troubleshooting ('install the pod network add-on')

claims.text: kind installs its own CNI plugin, kindnet, by default in every cluster it builds (it can be turned off with disableDefaultCNI); donhang's kind-config.yaml does not turn it off.
claims.source_hint: kind.sigs.k8s.io: Configuration > Networking (Disable Default CNI: 'kind ships with a simple networking implementation (kindnetd)'); deploy/k8s/kind-config.yaml at stage-3

claims.text: kindnet runs one Pod on every node, control-plane included, in kube-system with label app=kindnet. A Pod can be set to use its node's network (spec.hostNetwork): it then has the node's address and needs no CNI plugin to start; kindnet's Pods do this.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/cni.txt at stage-3; Pod API reference (PodSpec.hostNetwork); kubernetes.io: Cluster-level PSS tutorial (kindnet flagged for host namespaces)

claims.text: Each kindnet Pod writes on its node one route per other node's Pod range (podCIDR), pointing at that node's address; the node's operating system then forwards Pod packets by those routes, and the kindnet Pod is not on the packet path.
claims.source_hint: Proposed prompt 08 capture: ip route on a worker with disableDefaultCNI (expect no 10.244.x.0/24 via lines); current routes: outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/cni.txt

claims.text: kind's nodes are containers on one Docker network, so each node reaches every other node's address directly, in one step, and plain routes are enough.
claims.source_hint: kind.sigs.k8s.io: Design > Initial (nodes as containers on the 'kind' Docker network); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/cni.txt (all node addresses in 172.22.0.0/16, dev eth0)

claims.text: A route only picks the next machine; the packet keeps the Pod address. Routers (machines joining networks, forwarding by their own routes) by default know nothing about Pod ranges; a plugin for such nodes can wrap Pod packets between node addresses, unwrapped on arrival.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Cluster Administration > Addons (Cilium: native routing or overlay/encapsulation; Calico: overlay or non-overlay, with or without BGP)

claims.text: The CNI plugin decides whether NetworkPolicies are enforced: the API server accepts and stores them regardless; a plugin without NetworkPolicy support blocks nothing.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies > Prerequisites ('implemented by the network plugin... creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller... will have no effect')

claims.text: The plugin is chosen when the cluster is built and serves every application on it, so choosing it is a decision about the cluster, not about one application.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Plugins ('You must use a CNI plugin that is compatible with your cluster and that suits your needs')

claims.text: In the captured ip route output, 'via' gives the next address, 'dev eth0' the node's interface on the Docker network, 'default' covers the rest; the worker's own Pod range (10.244.2.0/24) has no 'via' line.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/cni.txt (no iproute2 docs root in versions.yaml)

claims.text: show (scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh, sourced by cni.sh) prints a command after '$' then runs it; kubectl there always uses context kind-donhang.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh and scripts/k8s/cni.sh lines 6-7 at stage-3

claims.text: cni.sh rebuilds the cluster donhang first if it is gone (lessons_cluster runs scripts/k8s/cluster-up.sh).
kindnet, kind's default CNI plugin, enforces NetworkPolicies on donhang (namespace donhang-staging).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-3 network-policy.txt (k8s.l3.network-policies: pg_isready goes from 'accepting connections' to 'no response' once policies sync)
